title: What if our biggest problems aren’t economic?
gist: Noah Smith argues that American discontent and political unrest are increasingly driven by non-economic needs — belonging, status, and respect — rather than material scarcity, citing data that Millennials did fine economically, that Trump's tariff and deportation policies failed on their own economic terms yet his base stuck with him, and that both parties' activist bases are motivated by cultural and foreign-policy concerns; he frames the 21st-century challenge as managing positional, zero-sum status competition.

insights.claim: Americans' dissatisfaction with their personal lives is rising alongside falling happiness surveys, slowly rising suicide, and consumer sentiment near record lows, even as the country enjoys robust jobs and moderate inflation.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A durable sentiment-fundamentals disconnect undermines the assumption that economic improvement lifts public mood — a caution for anyone reading consumer confidence as a demand signal.
insights.quote: analysts have struggled to figure out why consumer sentiment — at least, as measured by UMich — is at all-time lows
insights.locator: With a robust job market, low-ish inflation

insights.claim: Commentators forced to explain low consumer sentiment amid a strong economy have fallen back on 'vibes,' which the author calls simply a label for our ignorance.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Reframes the sentiment puzzle as a genuine measurement/theory gap, warning against treating 'vibes' as an explanation when modeling consumer behavior.
insights.quote: commentators have been reduced to talking about “vibes” — basically a label for our ignorance
insights.locator: With a robust job market, low-ish inflation

insights.claim: Corinth and Larrimore (2026) find Millennials had real median household income 20% higher than the previous generation — a slowdown from the Silent Generation (36%) and Boomers (26%) but similar to Gen X (16%) — largely explained by stalled growth in women's work hours, with lifetime income gains far outweighing higher education costs.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Hard generational-income data undercuts the 'screwed Millennials' narrative that underpins demands for redistribution, reshaping how to read the political economy of the Democratic base.
insights.quote: Millennials had a real median household income that was 20% higher than that of the previous generation

insights.claim: By their mid-30s Millennials' market income (before redistribution, cost-of-living adjusted) was well ahead of Gen X and Boomers and they had caught up in wealth, weakening the economic-grievance explanation for left-Millennial politics.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: If the base isn't economically deprived, redistribution-focused policy may not resolve its discontent, changing the calculus for what wins those voters.
insights.quote: By the time they hit their mid 30s, their market income was well ahead of Gen X or the Boomers

insights.claim: The universal health insurance that lefty Millennials most demand does not address the risks they actually experienced in their youth — unemployment and wage declines — suggesting their policy demands are misaligned with their stated grievances.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A mismatch between demanded policy and experienced risk hints the real driver is non-economic, informing where political energy actually comes from.
insights.quote: the kind of economic policies lefty Millennials demand — especially universal health insurance — don’t really address the main kinds of risks they experienced in their youth

themes.theme: Trump's economic policies failed on their own terms

insights.claim: Manufacturing employment has fallen since Trump took office and imposed broad tariffs, contradicting the promise that blue-collar jobs would return.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Tariff policy failing to reshore manufacturing jobs is a concrete rebuttal to the industrial-policy case, relevant to trade-exposed sectors and the political durability of protectionism.
insights.quote: Manufacturing employment has fallen since Trump took office and started putting tariffs on anyone and everyone

insights.claim: Mass deportations and a near-cessation of net immigration failed to raise native-born employment, with prime-age employment rates for native-born Americans falling to their lowest in more than four years.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The core labor-market case for restrictionism is empirically failing, evidence relevant to sectors dependent on immigrant labor and to the politics of immigration.
insights.quote: mass deportations and a near-cessation of net immigration to the U.S. have spectacularly failed to raise employment rates for native-born Americans

insights.claim: Trump's approval is low and inflation is the issue voters are most angry at him over, yet his base has stuck with him, which the author reads as strong evidence that economics was not their primary concern.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: If the coalition holds despite economic disappointment, the driver is sociocultural — reshaping how to forecast political outcomes and their policy consequences.
insights.quote: the fact that Trump’s base has stuck with him strongly implies that economics was not their primary concern
insights.locator: So it’s possible that Trump’s voters

insights.claim: The 2016 debate over whether Trump's win was 'economic anxiety' versus sociocultural issues resolved against economics; Margalit (2019) found economic insecurity explains only a modest share of populist support and that immigration concern is only marginally shaped by its economic repercussions.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The academic consensus that culture, not economics, drives populism is load-bearing for predicting which policies actually move voters.
insights.quote: the share of populist support explained by economic insecurity is modest

insights.claim: David Shor's analysis and the Enos-Hirsch (2015) finding show Democratic staffers are far to the left of median voters: 23% of Obama staffers named income inequality the single most important issue versus fewer than 1% of voters citing the rich-poor gap.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A large activist-vs-voter priority gap means party agendas may be set by preferences most voters don't share — a structural source of electoral misfire.
insights.quote: 23 percent of Obama staffers cited income inequality as the single most important issue facing the country, whereas polls from that election cycle found that fewer than one percent of all voters listed “the gap between rich and poor” as the most important issue

insights.claim: Jay Caspian Kang's 'Great Disappointed' Gen Z voters have coalesced around the war in Gaza as a character test rather than the economy, and prominent DSA organizers turn out to be scions of wealthy families — indicating an activist left that is effectively post-economic.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: If the energized left is motivated by foreign policy and identity rather than material grievance, economic policy is the wrong lever to court or predict them.
insights.quote: their political views have seemingly coalesced less around the economy than around the war in Gaza
insights.locator: In fact, in his essay, Kang describes

insights.claim: With most Americans possessing basic necessities and historically high economic security, many may have climbed Maslow's hierarchy to prioritize belonging, status, and respect over adding to their bank accounts, so boosting economic fortunes could barely move their happiness.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: If discontent is post-material, GDP- and jobs-oriented policy loses its grip on public mood — a structural reframe for reading political risk and sentiment.
insights.quote: the great challenge of the 21st century may be to make everyone feel high-status at the same time
insights.locator: It seems plausible to think that a great many Americans

insights.claim: Status is a positional, zero-sum good — one group's rise requires another's fall — so a world dominated by positional competition is inherently zero-sum and resistant to the win-win framing economics prefers.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A zero-sum status framework predicts persistent resentment that growth cannot dissolve, a lens for understanding durable social and political conflict.
insights.quote: A world dominated by positional goods — where one person having more requires that someone else have less — is a dark, zero-sum world.
insights.locator: And some of these psychological needs are positional goods

insights.claim: Inflation fell from 9% in summer 2022 to 3% in summer 2023 yet voters still punished Democrats in 2024, and inflation under Trump never approached 2022 levels yet voters remain furious — evidence that measured economic improvement no longer buys political credit.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A breakdown in the inflation-to-approval transmission complicates using macro data to forecast electoral and policy outcomes.
insights.quote: even though inflation fell from 9% in the summer of 2022 to just 3% in the summer of 2023, voters still seemed to punish Democrats at the polls in 2024
